metadata.title: Twenty dots beat "twenty percent"
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why natural frequencies and 20-dot quantile dotplots beat abstract percentages for communicating risk and uncertainty. Lands the carry-out that position and count replace mental arithmetic with direct perception.
metadata.anchor_pair: B04 / B05 -> B07 (The 1,000-person grid splitting into positive tests, resolving into the 20-dot quantile dotplot)
metadata.one_flag: B08 — showing twenty dots removes the translation tax; it does not decide risk tolerance
metadata.mirror_pair: B09 (both directions: raw percentage miscalibration vs extreme base rate dot grid scalability limits)

beats.narration_text: When we report model uncertainty or diagnostic risk, we default to percentages. Twenty percent chance of failure. Ninety percent accuracy. But percentages force mental arithmetic that human intuition consistently botches. Twenty dots beat twenty percent every time. Let's trace why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on "clearest way to report it?", corrects to "a trap for human intuition?"

props.text:
When communicating model uncertainty,
isn't 20% probability
the clearest way to report it?
props.triggerWords: the clearest way to report it?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Liam reads over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: Consider Gerd Gigerenzer's famous study of experienced physicians. They were given standard mammography statistics: ninety percent sensitivity, a nine point nine percent false-positive rate, and a baseline prevalence of roughly eight in one thousand. When asked the chance a positive patient actually has cancer, most estimated eighty to ninety percent.

shot.new_visual_element: The Physician Diagnostic Study: 90% Sensitivity vs 80-90% Perceived Risk

production_viz.label: The Physician Diagnostic Study
production_viz.mechanic: Physicians wildly overestimate cancer odds given sensitivity and false-positive percentages.

beats.narration_text: The standard reaction is that physicians are bad at probability, and that professionals simply need more training in statistical formulas. But when Gigerenzer presented the exact same medical facts as counts of people rather than normalized percentages, correct answers jumped from under twenty percent to over eighty percent.

shot.new_visual_element: The Wrong Prior: Doctors Need More Algebra vs Natural Frequencies Fix It Instantly

production_viz.label: The Representation Shift
production_viz.mechanic: Falsifying the assumption that physicians are bad at math by changing the framing from percentages to counts.

beats.narration_text: Percentages conceal population scale. Ninety percent sensitivity sounds overwhelming, while a ten percent false-positive rate sounds harmless. But because the disease is rare, ten percent of a massive healthy population produces roughly one hundred false alarms, completely swamping the eight genuine cases.

shot.new_visual_element: The Percentage Fog: Normalized Ratios Hide the Base Rate Disparity

production_viz.label: The Percentage Fog
production_viz.mechanic: Explaining how normalized rates obscure the 992-to-8 base rate imbalance.

beats.narration_text: Picture one thousand women screened for cancer. Grounded as countable individuals, the data splits immediately. Only eight women actually have the disease. Nine hundred and ninety-two women are healthy.

shot.new_visual_element: 1,000 Individuals: The Population Grid Splits into 8 Sick vs 992 Healthy

production_viz.label: The 1,000-Person Grid
production_viz.mechanic: Planting the visual anchor: a 1,000-person grid splitting into disease vs healthy sub-populations.

beats.narration_text: Now run the screening test. The eight cancer cases split: roughly seven or eight test positive. The healthy group splits: ninety-nine test positive as false alarms. Fade the negative tests. In the positive room, roughly eight out of one hundred and seven people are sick. That is under ten percent, visible at a single glance.

shot.new_visual_element: The Screening Split: False Alarms Swamping True Positives in the Positive Cohort

production_viz.label: The Screening Split
production_viz.mechanic: Splitting positive from negative test results to reveal the true posterior odds without algebra.

beats.narration_text: This works because of how the human visual system decodes information. In the Cleveland–McGill perception hierarchy, abstract percentages and color shading require error-prone mental computation. Spatial position and discrete item counts sit at the absolute top, decoded effortlessly without arithmetic.

shot.new_visual_element: The Cleveland-McGill Perception Hierarchy: Position & Count at the Apex

production_viz.label: The Perception Hierarchy
production_viz.mechanic: Ranking perceptual channels: position and count vs area and color saturation.

beats.narration_text: This brings us to the quantile dotplot. If your AI model has a twenty percent probability of failure, reporting "twenty percent risk" sounds like an abstract quibble. Showing twenty dots with exactly four filled transforms an elusive percentage into a concrete count: out of twenty deployments, expect about four failures.

shot.new_visual_element: The Quantile Dotplot: 20 Dots with 4 Filled and Natural Frequency Narration

production_viz.label: The Quantile Dotplot
production_viz.mechanic: Paying off the anchor with a 20-dot quantile dotplot (4 filled) and natural frequency caption.

beats.narration_text: Here is the essential distinction. Showing twenty dots removes the translation tax; it does not make the decision for you. Four filled dots give stakeholders an accurate grasp of the odds, but human judgment must still decide whether four failures in twenty is acceptable.

shot.new_visual_element: One Flag: The Boundary Between Perception and Judgment

production_viz.label: The Translation Boundary
production_viz.mechanic: Explicit inference flag marking where visual perception ends and human value judgment begins.

beats.narration_text: Both limits matter. Relying on raw percentages guarantees miscalibration, because human working memory confuses conditional test rates with actual posterior odds. But quantile dotplots also fail when base rates are extreme, where representing one failure in a million either forces rounding or an unreadable sea of dots.

shot.new_visual_element: Both Directions: Percentage Confusion vs Dot Grid Scalability Limits

production_viz.label: Both Failure Directions
production_viz.mechanic: Evaluating both sides: the cognitive trap of percentages vs the denominator limits of dotplots.

beats.narration_text: Position and count replace mental arithmetic with direct perception.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take one critical failure rate or diagnostic risk in your system currently reported as a percentage. Redesign it as a twenty-dot quantile dotplot with natural-frequency narration underneath: out of twenty cases, expect about N. Test both on a non-technical stakeholder. Does their risk assessment change? Liam, in for Bear.
